extracted.intended_audience: student reporters and newspaper writers / journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional guidance and examples on composing different types of newspaper news items (court reports, business/receivership pieces, human-interest features, local follow-ups), showing how to choose style, lead, and details for different audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring out human interest in routine news
rubrics_metrics.description: Note — The way in which the human interest can be brought out in what might ordinarily be considered routine news, is shown by the second of the following two stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human-interest treatment to make otherwise routine or technical items engaging. Illustrated by the two versions of the 'Patent Award' story: a straight factual account versus a narrative about Albert Janin leaving his job, family reaction, and local celebration. Employ personal anecdotes, domestic scenes, and emotional details to connect readers to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localize national or out-of-town stories (use a local hook)
rubrics_metrics.description: Note — The provisum in the will given in the New York court story making bequests to Chicago nurses formed the basis of the local story in the Chicago paper; both stories follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting a wider-interest story for a local paper, emphasize elements that tie the story to the paper's readership (local beneficiaries, local witnesses, hometown reactions). Produce a distinct local angle or follow-up that highlights the community connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize 'developments of the day' in concise points
rubrics_metrics.description: Developments of the day were as follows: (followed by numbered/pointed items describing receiver actions, bank conferences, minority creditor moves, investigations, appointments, statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ongoing or complex business/court stories, provide a clear, concise chronological summary of key developments. Use short bullet/numbered items or paragraph leads that list actions taken, investigations launched, appointments made, and relevant statements to bring readers up to date quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose reporting style appropriately: factual report vs. human-interest narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between the New York Times' factual 'Patent Award' report and the New York Evening World's narrative, scene-driven version showing Janin's personal reaction and community celebration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to write a straightforward, document-centered account (who, what, when, legal/technical facts) or a feature-style narrative (scene, dialogue, character detail). Match style to audience and the story's news value—use straight reporting for legal/technical authority and human-interest features to engage readers emotionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include precise concrete details (names, amounts, dates, positions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories include exact figures and specifics (e.g., bequests of $500, $1,500, estate valuations of $800,000–$1,000,000, receivership debts of nearly $2,600,000), names of people, dates, and official titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide exact, verifiable facts—figures, dates, full names, offices/titles—both for credibility and informativeness. In probate, business failure, or legal reporting, detail amounts, beneficiaries, corporate holdings, and formal actions (assignments, appointments) to allow readers to grasp scale and consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scene-setting and direct quotations to humanize and dramatize
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show scene detail (Janin taking off his apron, the foreman wringing his hand, a family celebration) and extensive direct quotes conveying feeling and intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with vivid scenes or short episodes and incorporate direct quotations to give voice to subjects. Scenes and quotes make abstract or technical matters tangible and help readers empathize with individuals involved.
